explanation: Why a unit failed, without paging through the whole journal. -u scopes to the unit, -n limits the lines, --no-pager keeps it in the pipeline.
Lists units that failed at boot. The first thing to run on a machine that came up wrong.
Shows what a unit will actually run, including drop-ins, after every override has been merged.
content: systemctl cat sshd.service && systemctl show sshd -p ExecStart

explanation: Ranks services by how long they delayed boot. The usual answer to a slow start is one unit near the top.
Largest directories at this level, human readable. -x stays on one filesystem so it does not wander into /proc or a mount.
A disk that reports free space but still refuses writes is usually out of inodes, not bytes.
Finds space held by deleted files that a process still has open. Deleting the file does not free the space until the handle closes.
The heaviest processes by resident memory. --sort takes a minus for descending order.
What a process is actually waiting on. Reading its file descriptors and stack says more than another look at top.
Traces the system calls a command makes, with a count and timing summary rather than a wall of output.
Listening sockets with the process behind each one. The modern replacement for netstat -tulpn.
Which route the kernel will actually use for a destination, including the source address it will pick.
Captures the start of connections only. -n skips DNS lookups, which otherwise generate the traffic you are trying to read.
Resolves a name through a specific server, which is how you tell a stale local cache from a stale zone.
World-writable files outside the places that are meant to be. A common way a service ends up modifiable by anyone.
Copies the ownership and mode of one file onto another, rather than typing the numbers and getting them wrong.
Accounts with a real login shell, which is the set that can actually sign in.
Accounts with an empty password field. Should return nothing on any machine you care about.
Reuses one connection for subsequent sessions, so every later ssh or scp to the same host skips the handshake.
Forwards a remote port to the local machine, so a service bound to localhost on the server is reachable here.
Mirrors a tree, deletes what no longer exists on the source, and shows what it would do first. Never run this without -n the first time.
Streams a directory to another host without a temporary archive on either side.
A cron entry that logs both streams. Without the redirect, cron mails the output to a mailbox nobody reads.
Removes stopped containers, unused networks and dangling images. The usual cause of a full disk on a build host.
